## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Akālarāvijātaka* (Ja 119) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework preserved in the commentary, the Buddha related this story while residing at Jetavana regarding a monk from Sāvatthī who failed to learn proper monastic duties and conduct, reciting and making noise at inappropriate hours of the night and thereby depriving other monks of sleep [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the story of the past, set in Bārāṇasī during the reign of King Brahmadatta, the Bodhisatta was born into a northern Brahmin family and became a world-renowned teacher (*disāpāmokkha ācariya*) instructing five hundred pupils [Fausböll 1877]. The core verse begins with the opening words *Amātāpitarisaṁvaddho*, reflecting upon a cock raised without parents or teacher that failed to know the proper time to crow [Fausböll 1877; Burlingame 1921]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identified the ill-timed cock with the disorderly monk, the pupils with the Buddha's disciples, and the teacher with himself [Fausböll 1877].

A version of the story is also preserved in the commentary to the Dhammapada under the name *Akālarāvi-kukkuṭa Jātaka*, where the Buddha relates the same verse in connection with Elder Padhānika Tissa, identifying the untimely cock as the Elder and the pupils as five hundred novices [Burlingame 1921].

No direct parallels in other Buddhist canonical traditions are cataloged by SuttaCentral, and automated text-reuse analyses by DharmaNexus found no Pali-internal reuse or cross-language matches meeting the significance threshold [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
